overview: The Ndebele kingdom developed in what is now Zimbabwe under Mzilikazi and his successor Lobengula. It incorporated people of different origins into a powerful regional state. This record concerns northern Ndebele history, rather than every community elsewhere bearing the Ndebele name.

periods.title: Mzilikazi’s kingdom
periods.summary: After migration from southern Africa, Mzilikazi established his kingdom in the Zimbabwe region by about 1840.

periods.title: Lobengula and conquest
periods.summary: Lobengula established Old Bulawayo in 1870. The British South Africa Company conquered the kingdom in 1893.

items.text: Mzilikazi left Zululand in 1822 and built a new state through migration, warfare and incorporation of other communities. By about 1840 it was established in the Zimbabwe region. The kingdom’s population was therefore more varied than a single royal genealogy suggests.

Lobengula founded Old Bulawayo in 1870, then left it in 1881 for a new capital near the present city. The old settlement was burned. The move means that an account simply saying “Bulawayo” needs a date before it can be placed accurately.

The Old Bulawayo heritage site includes the Indaba tree, associated with public affairs, and the location of a Jesuit mission. These features put discussion and religious encounters beside royal residences in the landscape of a capital.

A museum reconstruction made in 1998 included eight beehive-shaped houses, the king’s residence, a wagon shed, palisade and cattle enclosure. These were modern reconstructions of a historical settlement; a destructive fire in 2010 became another chapter in the site’s history.

sections.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand

items.text: Research on Old Bulawayo pottery draws on comparison with Ndebele potters and household practice. Vessel shapes can suggest different jobs, but the comparison must be tested against excavated remains. A broken pot is useful evidence precisely because researchers ask how it was actually used.

The comparative research describes imbiza vessels used in cooking porridge and preparing beer. Other vessels are associated with serving beer and ceremonies. A family’s pottery collection could therefore connect everyday food preparation with larger gatherings and ritual obligations.

Soot can help investigators recognize cooking pots, but it can also hide decoration. Archaeologists must look past a vessel’s dirty surface to understand both use and design. The washing-up that nobody finished can become a clue centuries later.

Aberdeen’s museum preserves a wooden straining spoon catalogued as Matabele. It is only 22.7 centimetres long, a kitchen-sized object rather than royal regalia. Its exact manufacture date is unrecorded, so it offers material context without being assigned to a particular year of Lobengula’s reign.

sections.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world

items.text: After conquest, Lobengula’s son Njube was educated at Zonnebloem in Cape Town. Colonial authorities resisted his return because of his political significance. Schooling in this case also separated a young man from home and placed limits on his freedom to travel.

Njube’s 1898 letters ask for money for books and mention debt from tram travel. These details show a student managing very ordinary expenses while living through extraordinary political upheaval. A royal family’s history can include a troublesome transport bill.

His 14 October 1898 English letter includes: “Will you please let me go Home fore Holiday”. In modern spelling, he asks permission to go home for a holiday. This is his attested written voice, including “fore”; it is not offered as an isiNdebele-language sample.

The British South Africa Company’s 1893 campaign was a war of conquest. Historian Paul Gundani examines how supporters used religious and moral arguments to justify it. Reading those arguments critically helps distinguish claims made by invaders from the consequences for the people they defeated.

ending.text: The kingdom lost its independence in the British South Africa Company’s conquest of 1893. Ndebele people and language continued beyond that defeat. The imported map interval extending to 1914 should not be read as another twenty-one years of independent royal government.
